title: Highlights from PG 16 to 18: uuidv7, virtual generated columns, OLD/NEW in RETURNING, temporal constraints, skip scan, async I/O, JSON_TABLE, MERGE ... RETURNING
summary: Three releases changed a lot of standing advice: UUID keys, generated columns, audit queries, non-overlap constraints, composite index design, JSON import and MERGE. A tour with small runnable proofs, each feature tagged with its version and linked to the lesson that covers it in depth.

examples.title: PG 18 table definitions: temporal keys, uuidv7, virtual columns, NOT NULL as constraints

annotations.note: btree_gist gives int a GiST equality operator class. For key columns that aren't ranges, the docs call adding it the expected way to use WITHOUT OVERLAPS.

PG 18 temporal primary key: requirement_id may repeat as long as the valid ranges don't overlap. It is enforced like the exclusion constraint you had to write by hand before 18 (requirement_id WITH =, valid WITH &&), and foreign keys can now reference it.

uuidv7() (PG 18) puts a timestamp in the leading bits, so new keys arrive roughly in order at the end of the B-tree instead of at random places. The old advice, gen_random_uuid() or the uuid-ossp extension, gives random v4 keys (sql.tables-types.ids).

No keyword now means VIRTUAL (PG 18): computed when read, no storage. Before 18 the STORED keyword was required, so old DDL can't silently change meaning. Virtual columns may use built-in functions and types only.

PG 18 temporal foreign key: the rows with the same requirement_id must together cover the whole ran period. The referenced key must be declared WITHOUT OVERLAPS, and ON DELETE CASCADE and friends aren't supported here.
This run spans the switch between two versions. Neither covers it alone; together they do, and that is what PERIOD checks.
uuid_extract_version (PG 17) reads the version back; duration_s is computed on read.
The temporal key's index is GiST, the uuid key's is B-tree. Also new in 18: every NOT NULL is a named row in pg_constraint (contype n), and ALTER TABLE can add one as NOT VALID.
attgenerated is 'v' for virtual, 's' for stored.
SQLSTATE 23P01, exclusion_violation: the docs describe WITHOUT OVERLAPS as enforced by an EXCLUDE constraint rather than a unique one, and the error says so. Catch 23P01 in Go, not 23505.

examples.title: IS JSON (16), JSON_TABLE (17), MERGE ... RETURNING (17) with old/new (18)

annotations.note: PG 16 IS JSON: validate text before casting it instead of catching a cast error. It can also test for ARRAY or SCALAR, and WITH UNIQUE KEYS.
PG 17 JSON_TABLE: the SQL-standard way to turn a JSON document into typed rows. Before 17 you combined jsonb_array_elements or jsonb_to_recordset with ->> per field (sql.json.path-table).
One statement: parse the CI report, merge it into test_cases and return what changed. A MERGE with RETURNING can sit in WITH like any data-modifying statement, which is how its output gets sorted.
TC-1 matches with an unchanged status: no action, so no RETURNING row.
PG 17 WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE acts on target rows the source doesn't mention. Before 17 that took a second statement.
merge_action() (PG 17) names the action behind each row; old and new (PG 18) give both sides, with old NULL for the insert. Before 17 a MERGE returned only its row count.

examples.title: Skip scan, EXPLAIN's new defaults, and the async I/O settings (PG 18)

annotations.note: status leads the index and the query never mentions it. Before 18 a B-tree could serve this query only by reading the whole index, so the advice was "filter column first, or a second index".
271 pages of index, for comparison with what the scan touches below.
The answer. Running the query once first also keeps one-time catalog lookups out of the EXPLAIN output below.

Index Searches: 7 (a PG 18 EXPLAIN line): the scan jumped from one status value to the next, touching 23 index buffers instead of 271 pages. Buffers appears without asking for it, and row counts print with two decimals: both new in 18.

PG 18 asynchronous I/O lets a backend queue several reads at once for sequential scans, bitmap heap scans and VACUUM. worker (the default) hands them to io_workers background processes; io_uring needs a Linux build with liburing; sync means no AIO. The effective_io_concurrency default rose to 16. A tuned server shows other values.

use_cases: Reviewing old advice before applying it: Stack Overflow answers, ORM defaults and blog posts written for PostgreSQL 9 to 15
Planning an upgrade: which features you gain, and which incompatibilities (the release notes' Migration section) you must handle
Choosing a minimum supported server version for software you ship, such as TraceLite on a customer's machine
strengths: Several features replace extensions or hand-written workarounds: uuidv7 instead of uuid-ossp, WITHOUT OVERLAPS instead of a hand-written EXCLUDE, JSON_TABLE instead of jsonb_to_recordset chains
RETURNING old/new and MERGE ... RETURNING make audit-style writes one statement, without triggers
Skip scan and async I/O speed up existing queries without changing them
One major version a year, five years of support for each, and fix-only minor releases at least every three months make upgrades plannable
weaknesses: Features depend on the server version, not on your client: code using uuidv7() fails on a PG 17 server with no compile-time warning
Defaults moved: generated columns are virtual unless you say STORED, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints BUFFERS, so old expected outputs and scripts can differ
Some new features are first versions: temporal foreign keys support no CASCADE or SET NULL actions, virtual columns can't use user-defined functions
Managed services and Linux distributions trail the newest release, so 'available in PostgreSQL' and 'available on your server' differ

pitfalls.title: Following advice without its version
pitfalls.detail: 'Use uuid-ossp for UUIDs', 'generated columns are always stored', 'MERGE can't return rows', 'a composite index is useless without its first column': each was true for some versions. Check the release notes for when it changed.

pitfalls.title: Using a feature newer than the oldest server you support
pitfalls.detail: Check at startup or in a migration, and fail with a clear message instead of a syntax error halfway through. server_version_num is an integer: 180007 for 18.7.

pitfalls.title: Catching unique violations from a temporal key
pitfalls.detail: A WITHOUT OVERLAPS conflict is an exclusion violation, SQLSTATE 23P01, not unique_violation 23505. Error mapping written for plain keys misses it and returns a 500.

pitfalls.title: Assuming a virtual column is indexed or stored
pitfalls.detail: Virtual is the default now. If you need to index the value or read it often from a large table, say STORED explicitly, as before 18.
pitfalls.good: price_gross int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (price_net * 120 / 100) STORED

quiz.q: On PG 18, `CREATE TABLE t (a int, b int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a * 2))` creates b as...
options: A syntax error: STORED is required
quiz.why: PG 18 made VIRTUAL the default. Before 18, STORED was required, so the same statement failed.

quiz.q: Which version added RETURNING to MERGE, and which added old/new in RETURNING?
quiz.why: PG 17 added MERGE ... RETURNING with merge_action(); PG 18 added the old and new aliases for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.

quiz.q: An index on (status, ran_on); the query filters only on ran_on. What changed in PG 18?
options: Nothing, the leading column must be constrained
The B-tree can skip from one status value to the next instead of reading the whole index
PostgreSQL creates a second index automatically
quiz.why: Skip scan lets multicolumn B-tree indexes be used without conditions on the leading columns; it pays off when those columns have few distinct values.

quiz.q: Inserting an overlapping period into a table with `PRIMARY KEY (id, valid WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` fails with which SQLSTATE?
quiz.why: WITHOUT OVERLAPS is enforced like an EXCLUDE constraint on a GiST index, so a conflict is an exclusion violation.

body:
## Concept

PostgreSQL ships one major version a year. Much of what you'll read online predates the
last three, and some of it is now wrong. The headline changes, with the old advice they
retire:

**PostgreSQL 16 (2023)**

- SQL/JSON constructors (`JSON_OBJECT`, `JSON_ARRAY`, `JSON_ARRAYAGG`,
  `JSON_OBJECTAGG`) and the `IS JSON` predicate.
- `ANY_VALUE()`; integer literals in hex, octal and binary (`0x1F`) and underscores in
  numbers (`1_000_000`); `pg_input_is_valid()` to test a cast without an error.
- `pg_stat_io` for I/O statistics; parallel `FULL` and right outer hash joins.

**PostgreSQL 17 (2024)**

- `JSON_TABLE` and `JSON_EXISTS`/`JSON_QUERY`/`JSON_VALUE`: "parse JSON in the app" is
  no longer the only clean option.
- `MERGE ... RETURNING` with `merge_action()`, `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`, and `MERGE`
  on updatable views.
- `COPY ... ON_ERROR ignore`, `transaction_timeout`, incremental backups, the
  `MAINTAIN` privilege, and the builtin `C.UTF-8` collation provider (the one local
  mode's playground database uses).

**PostgreSQL 18 (2025)**

- `uuidv7()`: time-ordered UUID keys without an extension.
- Generated columns are **virtual** by default.
- `RETURNING old.*, new.*` in `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `MERGE`.
- Temporal constraints: `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE ... WITHOUT OVERLAPS` and foreign keys
  with `PERIOD`.
- B-tree **skip scan**; an **asynchronous I/O** subsystem; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes
  `BUFFERS` by default.
- `NOT NULL` constraints stored in `pg_constraint` (nameable, addable `NOT VALID`);
  `CHECK` and foreign keys can be `NOT ENFORCED`; `pg_upgrade` keeps planner
  statistics; `casefold()`; MD5 passwords deprecated; data checksums on by default in
  new clusters.

The examples prove the ones you'll touch in everyday schema and query work; the linked
lessons go deeper.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Language versions:** like checking whether advice targets Java 8 or Java 21, or
  Go before 1.22's loop variable change, check which PostgreSQL version a piece of SQL
  advice assumes. The go.timeline lesson does the same tour for Go.
- **Runtime, not compile time:** a Go program built with a newer toolchain still runs;
  SQL that uses `uuidv7()` fails on a PG 17 server at execution. The database is the
  runtime, and its version is a deployment fact your code should check.
- **Release cadence:** one major version a year, each supported for five years, with
  fix-only minor releases at least every three months. Minor upgrades (18.6 to 18.7) are
  binary replacements; major upgrades go through `pg_upgrade`, dump and restore, or
  logical replication.

## Design notes

Decide a minimum server version deliberately and write it down, as this curriculum does
with `since`. For an application you host, take the newest major version your platform
offers; for software installed on someone else's machine (TraceLite's packaging step),
support what they can realistically run and check `server_version_num` at startup.

Read the "Migration to Version N" section of each release's notes before upgrading: it
lists the incompatibilities, such as the virtual default for generated columns, MD5
deprecation warnings, `AFTER` triggers running as the queuing role, and `VACUUM` and
`ANALYZE` processing inheritance children by default in 18.

Adopt new features where they remove code or extensions: `uuidv7()` for new
UUID-keyed tables, `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` for validity periods, `RETURNING old/new` for
audit-style writes, `JSON_TABLE` for imports. Don't rewrite working code just because a
newer form exists, and keep the old idiom in mind when you read other people's schemas.

files.examples/01_pg18_tables.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.modern.16-to-18): three PG 18 features in two table definitions.
-- WITHOUT OVERLAPS needs GiST equality for the int column: btree_gist.
CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;

-- Temporal primary key: many rows per requirement, but no two periods overlap.
CREATE TABLE requirement_versions (
  requirement_id int,
  valid          daterange,
  title          text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (requirement_id, valid WITHOUT OVERLAPS)
);
INSERT INTO requirement_versions VALUES
  (1, '[2026-01-01,2026-06-01)', 'Giriş'),
  (1, '[2026-06-01,)',           'Giriş, SSO dahil');

CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id             uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),   -- time-ordered UUID
  requirement_id int  NOT NULL,
  ran            daterange NOT NULL,
  duration_ms    int  NOT NULL,
  duration_s     numeric(6,2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (duration_ms / 1000.0),  -- virtual
  -- Temporal foreign key: the requirement must exist for the whole period.
  FOREIGN KEY (requirement_id, PERIOD ran)
    REFERENCES requirement_versions (requirement_id, PERIOD valid)
);
INSERT INTO test_runs (requirement_id, ran, duration_ms) VALUES
  (1, '[2026-03-10,2026-03-11)', 1500),
  (1, '[2026-05-31,2026-06-02)', 2250);  -- spans both versions: still covered

SELECT uuid_extract_version(id) AS uuid_version, ran, duration_ms, duration_s
FROM test_runs
ORDER BY ran;

-- The catalog: a GiST index behind the temporal key, NOT NULL as a
-- constraint row (contype n), and a virtual generated column.
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS tbl, c.conname, c.contype,
       CASE c.contype WHEN 'p' THEN am.amname END AS key_index
FROM pg_constraint c
LEFT JOIN pg_class i ON i.oid = c.conindid
LEFT JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid = i.relam
WHERE c.conrelid IN ('requirement_versions'::regclass, 'test_runs'::regclass)
ORDER BY c.conrelid::regclass::text, c.conname;
SELECT attname, attgenerated FROM pg_attribute
WHERE attrelid = 'test_runs'::regclass AND attgenerated <> '';

-- An overlapping period is rejected like an exclusion-constraint conflict.
INSERT INTO requirement_versions VALUES (1, '[2026-05-01,2026-07-01)', 'Çakışan');
files.examples/02_json_merge.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_cases (code text PRIMARY KEY, status text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES ('TC-1', 'passed'), ('TC-2', 'failed'), ('TC-3', 'failed');

-- PG 16: IS JSON checks text before you cast it.
SELECT doc, doc IS JSON OBJECT AS is_object
FROM (VALUES ('{"case": "TC-1"}'), ('[1, 2]'), ('{"case": ')) AS v(doc)
ORDER BY doc;

-- A CI job reports its results as one JSON document.
CREATE TABLE ci_reports (id int PRIMARY KEY, body jsonb NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES (1, '{"results": [
  {"case": "TC-1", "status": "passed"},
  {"case": "TC-2", "status": "passed"},
  {"case": "TC-4", "status": "failed"}]}');

-- PG 17: JSON_TABLE turns the document into rows.
SELECT r.*
FROM ci_reports,
     JSON_TABLE(body, '$.results[*]'
       COLUMNS (code text PATH '$.case', status text PATH '$.status')) AS r
ORDER BY r.code;

-- PG 17: MERGE with WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE and RETURNING merge_action();
-- PG 18: old/new in RETURNING.
WITH changes AS (
  MERGE INTO test_cases t
  USING (SELECT r.* FROM ci_reports,
           JSON_TABLE(body, '$.results[*]'
             COLUMNS (code text PATH '$.case', status text PATH '$.status')) AS r
         WHERE ci_reports.id = 1) AS r
  ON t.code = r.code
  WHEN MATCHED AND t.status <> r.status THEN UPDATE SET status = r.status
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (r.code, r.status)
  WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN UPDATE SET status = 'not run'
  RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.code, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status
)
SELECT * FROM changes ORDER BY code;
